title: Big Changes: Dead Zones, Storms and Climate

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: What is a dead zone in the Chesapeake Bay lesson?
cards.back: Deep water with less than 2 mg/L of dissolved oxygen.
cards.why: It is not lifeless: bacteria live there.
cards.quote: In this lesson, a dead zone has less than 2 mg/L of dissolved oxygen.
cards.section: Explain: how extra nutrients use up oxygen

cards.front: {{c1::Dissolved oxygen}} is oxygen gas mixed into water, measured in milligrams per liter (mg/L).
cards.quote: Dissolved oxygen is oxygen gas mixed into water.
cards.section: Explain: how extra nutrients use up oxygen

cards.front: Which two nutrients do algae need that come from fertilizer, manure, wastewater and some air pollution?
cards.back: Nitrogen and phosphorus.
cards.quote: Algae need nitrogen and phosphorus, which come from fertilizer, manure, wastewater and some air pollution.
cards.section: Explain: how extra nutrients use up oxygen

cards.front: A {{c1::decomposer}} breaks down dead matter. Many bacteria are decomposers, and they use oxygen while they do it.
cards.quote: A decomposer breaks down dead matter.
cards.section: Explain: how extra nutrients use up oxygen

cards.front: What is eutrophication?
cards.back: Extra nutrients in water feeding too much algae growth, which can lead to low oxygen.
cards.quote: Eutrophication is extra nutrients in water feeding too much algae growth, which can lead to low oxygen.
cards.section: Explain: how extra nutrients use up oxygen

cards.front: In a summer dead zone in the Bay, what uses up most of the oxygen in the deep water, and why is the oxygen not replaced?
cards.back: Decomposers breaking down dead algae use it up. The deep water mixes poorly, so little new oxygen comes down.
cards.quote: Extra nutrients feed algae, and decomposers breaking down the dead algae use up oxygen in deep water that mixes poorly.
cards.section: Explain: how extra nutrients use up oxygen

cards.front: Fertilizer runs into a bay. Why is it wrong to say the fertilizer itself takes oxygen from the water?
cards.back: Fertilizer only feeds algae. Decomposers breaking down the dead algae are what use the deep oxygen.
cards.quote: Fertilizer does not take oxygen from the Bay by itself: its nutrients feed algae, and decomposers use the deep oxygen.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: In the Bay model, deep water is low on oxygen and a big storm mixes the surface and deep layers for a few days. What happens to deep oxygen, and is the problem solved?
cards.back: Deep oxygen rises for a time as surface oxygen moves down. The problem is not solved: the nutrients and dead algae remain.
cards.why: A storm brings deep oxygen back only for a time.
cards.quote: It rises for a time as surface oxygen moves down. The nutrients and dead algae remain.
cards.section: Explain: how extra nutrients use up oxygen

cards.front: Why do summer dead zones in the Bay usually end in fall?
cards.back: Cooler water and winds usually mix the Bay in fall, so oxygen returns to the deep water.
cards.quote: In fall, cooler water and winds usually mix the Bay, and oxygen returns to the deep water.
cards.section: Explain: losing variety, and coming back

cards.front: A farmer spreads a lot of fertilizer on a field next to a creek. That night heavy rain falls. What is most likely to happen downstream, and why?
cards.back: Algae may grow fast in the creek and river water. Rain washes fertilizer off the field, and its nutrients feed the algae.
cards.why: Nutrients from land can wash into water.
cards.quote: Algae need nitrogen and phosphorus, which come from fertilizer, manure, wastewater and some air pollution.
cards.section: Explain: how extra nutrients use up oxygen

cards.front: A student says, "Nutrients are good for living things, so lots of fertilizer in a pond will help the fish." Give the best reply.
cards.back: Wrong. Extra nutrients feed many algae. When the algae die, decomposers use up the oxygen that fish need.
cards.quote: Many bacteria are decomposers, and they use oxygen while breaking down dead algae
cards.section: Explain: how extra nutrients use up oxygen

cards.front: What is the difference between a climate change and a catastrophic disturbance?
cards.back: A climate change is a lasting shift in a place's usual temperature, rain or weather over many years. A catastrophic disturbance is a sudden event, such as a hurricane, flood or forest fire, that harms many living things at once.
cards.quote: A catastrophic disturbance is a sudden event, such as a hurricane, flood or forest fire, that harms many living things at once.
cards.section: Explain: climate changes and sudden disasters

cards.front: {{c1::Biodiversity}} is the variety of living things in an area.
cards.quote: Biodiversity is the variety of living things in an area.
cards.section: Explain: losing variety, and coming back

cards.front: Does a big disturbance lower every kind of life? Give the Puerto Rico forest example.
cards.back: No. Researchers cut treetops to copy a hurricane. More kinds of plants grew there, while several animal groups became less common.
cards.quote: A review reported that more kinds of plants grew there, while several animal groups became less common.
cards.section: Explain: losing variety, and coming back

cards.front: A pine forest burns. Fifteen years later, before the young trees make many seeds, it burns again. What is the best prediction?
cards.back: Fewer young trees may grow back than after one fire. In Yellowstone, forests that burned twice in a short time had about one sixth as many young trees.
cards.quote: Forests that burn again before they recover, like the second film's, may not grow back the same way.
cards.section: Explain: losing variety, and coming back

cards.front: The lesson compares an ecosystem to a rubber band. What does the comparison say about small and large changes, and where does it break down?
cards.back: A small stretch may reverse, while a large one may leave a lasting change. Unlike a band, a changed ecosystem can still work, just differently.
cards.quote: An ecosystem is a bit like a rubber band: a small stretch may reverse, while a large one may leave a lasting change.
cards.section: Explain: losing variety, and coming back

cards.front: What are two things that decide whether an ecosystem recovers or shifts after a big change?
cards.back: How severe the change is, and how long it lasts.
cards.quote: Big changes can lower biodiversity, and an ecosystem may recover or shift depending on how severe a change is and how long it lasts.
cards.section: Explain: losing variety, and coming back

cards.front: Bay data: 2019 had 77.5 million kg of spring nitrogen and an 11.6 km³ dead zone. 2023 had 33.1 million kg and 1.5 km³. How much more nitrogen came in 2019, and about how many times larger was the dead zone?
cards.back: Nitrogen: 77.5 - 33.1 = 44.4 million kg more. Dead zone: 11.6 / 1.5 is about 7.7 times larger.
cards.quote: Compare 2019 with 2023. How much more nitrogen came in, and how much larger was the dead zone?
cards.section: Elaborate: read eight years of Bay numbers

cards.front: Bay summer dead-zone volumes for 2017 to 2024 (km³): 1.9, 4.8, 11.6, 3.5, 3.7, 5.1, 1.5, 3.9. What is the mean?
cards.back: The sum is 36.0 km³. Divided by 8 years, the mean is 4.5 km³.
cards.quote: Find the mean dead-zone volume.
cards.section: Elaborate: read eight years of Bay numbers

cards.front: In one Bay year, one year had both the most spring nitrogen and the largest dead zone. Does that prove nitrogen was the only cause?
cards.back: No. Wind, temperature and mixing matter too. Wet springs also add fresh water, which can strengthen the layers.
cards.quote: Wind, temperature and mixing matter too. Wet springs also add fresh water, which can strengthen the layers.
cards.section: Elaborate: read eight years of Bay numbers

cards.front: Bay data: 2017 had 43.5 million kg of spring nitrogen and a 1.9 km³ dead zone. 2021 had 40.6 million kg and 3.7 km³. What is the best conclusion?
cards.back: Nitrogen matters, but other things change the dead zone too. 2021 had a little less nitrogen but a larger dead zone, so other things, such as wind, temperature or mixing, can matter too.
cards.why: Rule used: one cause does not act alone.
cards.quote: Wind, temperature and mixing matter too. Wet springs also add fresh water, which can strengthen the layers.
cards.section: Elaborate: read eight years of Bay numbers

cards.front: A pond-jar test uses one jar each of 0, 1, 2 and 4 drops of fertilizer per liter. What problem remains, and what fixes it?
cards.back: One unusual jar could mislead you. Use three jars per amount and find each mean, so repeats show whether the pattern holds.
cards.quote: One unusual jar could mislead you. Repeats show whether the pattern holds.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the jar test, which result would support the claim that extra nutrients lead to low oxygen, and why is the test only a model?
cards.back: Greener jars that later test lower in oxygen support it. Jars are a model with no layers or tides.
cards.quote: Meaning: greener jars that later test lower in oxygen support the chain. Jars are a model with no layers or tides.
cards.section: Design problem
